title: Practice Set 1 — Why Spark Exists
description: Test your understanding of distributed computing fundamentals, Spark's architecture, and the NordGrid Energy pipeline. This foundation practice set focuses on concept identification and output prediction — the building blocks you will need before writing PySpark code in Module 2.

description.context: Single-machine processing has three physical walls. The MEMORY wall is the limit on how much data fits in RAM at once — when a program tries to load more bytes than RAM can hold, the OS raises a MemoryError. The DISK I/O wall is how fast bytes can be read from storage — slow disks make jobs SLOW, not CRASHED. The COMPUTE wall is how many rows the CPU can process per second — slow CPUs also produce SLOW jobs, not CRASHES. Memory is the only wall that produces a hard crash at the LOADING stage, before any computation runs. Pandas in particular expands raw bytes into Python objects (each string becomes ~50 bytes of overhead), so 120 GB of CSV typically needs 3-5x that in RAM.
description.task: Which wall crashed the script, and why is the crash unavoidable on this server?
description.validationHint: Only one of the three walls explains a crash that happens at the data-loading stage, before any computation begins.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: pd.read_csv('scada_telemetry/2025_full_year/*.csv')

Hardware: 32 GB RAM, SSD (500 MB/s), 8 CPU cores. Input: 120 GB of SCADA CSV across 2,000 turbines.

evidence.label: Error output
evidence.content:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "load_scada.py", line 4, in <module>
    df = pd.read_csv('scada_telemetry/2025_full_year/*.csv')
MemoryError: Unable to allocate array

fields.label: Which processing wall caused the crash?
options: Disk I/O — the SSD reads 120 GB at 500 MB/s, which takes ~4 minutes; the timeout for a Python read raises MemoryError after 60 seconds.
Memory — Pandas tries to load all 120 GB into RAM at once, but the server only has 32 GB. The OS denies the allocation and Python raises MemoryError before any rows are processed.
Compute — 2,000 turbines × 8,760 hourly rows is too many records for 8 CPU cores to parse, so Python aborts the load with MemoryError.
All three walls hit simultaneously when the data exceeds the machine's combined capacity, and Python raises MemoryError as the most general error.
fields.correctAnswer: Memory — Pandas tries to load all 120 GB into RAM at once, but the server only has 32 GB. The OS denies the allocation and Python raises MemoryError before any rows are processed.
fields.rationale: MemoryError at the read_csv line is the signature of the memory wall: the program asked the OS for more RAM than exists, and the OS refused.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Confuses slow reads with crashes; Python does not have a 60-second read timeout that raises MemoryError.

fields.label: Why is this crash unavoidable on the development server?
options: Because the SSD cannot read 120 GB in a reasonable time, so Python gives up and raises MemoryError to signal the read failed.
Because 120 GB of raw CSV expands 3-5x when Pandas converts strings to Python objects; the working set is 400+ GB, far beyond the 32 GB RAM limit.
Because the 8 CPU cores cannot keep up with the parser, so Pandas falls behind and the read buffer overflows into a MemoryError.
Because Python has a built-in 32 GB file size limit on read_csv that triggers MemoryError when the input exceeds it.
fields.correctAnswer: Because 120 GB of raw CSV expands 3-5x when Pandas converts strings to Python objects; the working set is 400+ GB, far beyond the 32 GB RAM limit.
fields.rationale: Pandas does not load the raw bytes — it converts each CSV cell into a Python object (PyObject overhead ~50 bytes per string, plus type metadata).
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Conflates slow reads with memory errors; SSD speed never causes MemoryError.

description.context: There are exactly two ways to give a slow data job more capacity. SCALE UP (vertical scaling) means buying a bigger single machine — more RAM, more cores, faster disk on ONE box. SCALE OUT (horizontal scaling) means connecting MULTIPLE machines into a cluster and splitting the work across them. A third option — rewriting the code in a faster language — is NOT scaling at all; it is code optimization, which only delays hitting the same physical walls. The crucial property of scale-out is that you can keep adding machines (linear, open-ended growth), while scale-up always hits a ceiling — the largest machine money can buy is finite.
description.task: Classify each proposal and pick the one that handles long-term data growth.
description.validationHint: Two proposals match a named scaling strategy. One proposal addresses a different concern entirely.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Three proposals to fix NordGrid's 35-minute daily meter pipeline (target: under 5 minutes).

evidence.label: Proposals
evidence.content:
Proposal A: Buy one server with 1 TB RAM, 128 cores, NVMe. Run the same Python script on it.
Proposal B: Cluster eight existing 64 GB servers; install Spark and split work across all eight.
Proposal C: Rewrite the Python pipeline in C++ for faster per-row processing. Same single server.

fields.label: What scaling strategy does Proposal A represent?
options: Scaling up — replacing one machine with a bigger machine (more RAM, more cores) is the textbook definition of vertical scaling.
Scaling out — buying premium hardware is what 'horizontal scaling' means in the cloud era.
Neither — buying hardware is a procurement decision, not a scaling strategy.
Both — a 1 TB server is so large that it counts as both vertical and horizontal scaling.
fields.correctAnswer: Scaling up — replacing one machine with a bigger machine (more RAM, more cores) is the textbook definition of vertical scaling.
fields.rationale: Scale-up = bigger single machine.Proposal A keeps the architecture identical (one machine, one Python process) and just makes the box bigger.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Confuses cost/premium with scale-out; horizontal scaling requires multiple machines, not one expensive one.

fields.label: What scaling strategy does Proposal B represent?
options: Scaling up — installing Spark gives each individual machine more capacity.
Scaling out — connecting eight machines and splitting work across them is the textbook definition of horizontal scaling.
Neither — Spark is a software change, not a scaling change.
Code optimization — Spark is a faster language than Python so it is in the same category as Proposal C.
fields.correctAnswer: Scaling out — connecting eight machines and splitting work across them is the textbook definition of horizontal scaling.
fields.rationale: Scale-out = multiple machines working together.Proposal B turns 8 separate boxes into one logical compute pool via Spark.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Spark does not change a machine's specs; it splits work ACROSS machines.

fields.label: What scaling strategy does Proposal C represent?
options: Scaling up — C++ uses memory more efficiently, so the same machine effectively has more RAM.
Scaling out — rewriting in C++ unlocks parallel execution that Python cannot do.
Neither — this is a code optimization. The hardware is unchanged, so the three physical walls are unchanged.
Both — faster code on the same hardware is equivalent to bigger hardware running the original code.
fields.correctAnswer: Neither — this is a code optimization. The hardware is unchanged, so the three physical walls are unchanged.
fields.rationale: Scaling is about HARDWARE capacity (RAM, cores, machines).Proposal C changes the SOFTWARE — same RAM, same cores, same disk.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: C++ is more memory-efficient but the RAM ceiling is unchanged; you eventually hit it with more data.

fields.label: Which proposal best addresses long-term growth as NordGrid doubles its meter fleet?
options: Proposal A — the 1 TB server is so big it will handle any future growth NordGrid can imagine.
Proposal B — the cluster can grow by adding more machines whenever data grows; this is open-ended and linear.
Proposal C — C++ keeps the code so efficient that even 10x data still fits on the original server.
All three — long-term growth is solved equally well by any approach as long as the pipeline finishes under 5 minutes today.
fields.correctAnswer: Proposal B — the cluster can grow by adding more machines whenever data grows; this is open-ended and linear.
fields.rationale: Scale-out is the only strategy with no ceiling.Proposal A hits a hard limit (the largest single machine on the market).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Has a finite ceiling; eventually no single machine is big enough.
Option C: Optimization delays but never eliminates the wall.

tasks.title: Predict Cluster Utilization for Turbine Data

description.context: Spark's parallelism model is one-to-one: ONE CORE processes ONE PARTITION at a time. If you have 8 cores and 12 partitions, the first batch occupies all 8 cores; when those finish, the remaining 4 partitions go to 4 cores while the other 4 cores sit idle. Spark never splits a single partition across multiple cores. This means the rule for designing partition counts is: TARGET 2-4x the number of cores, so the cluster stays busy and stragglers do not hold up the whole job. With FEWER partitions than cores, you waste cores that have nothing to do.
description.task: Predict the cluster behavior across the three scenarios.
description.validationHint: Remember that each core processes one partition at a time, and Spark assigns new partitions to cores as they finish.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Cluster: 4 executors x 2 cores = 8 total cores. Input: SCADA file split into 12 partitions of equal size.

fields.label: How many partitions can Spark process simultaneously in the first batch?
fields.rationale: 8 cores available, 12 partitions to process. The first batch fills all 8 cores with 1 partition each.

fields.label: After the first batch of 8 partitions completes, how many cores sit idle while the remaining partitions are processed?
fields.rationale: 12 - 8 = 4 remaining partitions. With 8 cores and only 4 partitions left, 4 cores are active and 4 sit idle.

fields.label: If the telemetry file were split into only 4 partitions instead of 12, what would happen?
options: All 8 cores stay busy — Spark automatically re-splits the 4 partitions into 8 sub-partitions to fill every core.
Only 4 cores process data; the other 4 sit idle for the entire job because Spark assigns one core per partition and never splits a partition.
The job fails with a 'partition count below core count' error because Spark requires partitions >= cores.
Spark combines cores so 2 cores work cooperatively on each of the 4 partitions, finishing twice as fast.
fields.correctAnswer: Only 4 cores process data; the other 4 sit idle for the entire job because Spark assigns one core per partition and never splits a partition.
fields.rationale: Spark's unit of parallel work is the partition; each partition is processed by exactly one core from start to finish.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Spark does not auto-repartition to match core count; you must explicitly call repartition().

tasks.title: Classify NordGrid's Datasets by Medallion Layer

description.context: The medallion architecture organizes data into three layers by HOW MUCH HAS BEEN DONE to it. BRONZE = raw landing zone — bytes are stored exactly as the source produced them, with all quality issues preserved (negative sensor values, nulls, duplicates). SILVER = cleaned and conformed — types are correct, invalid rows are removed, reference data is joined in, but the GRANULARITY is still individual records (one row per meter per day, one row per turbine per hour). GOLD = aggregated and business-ready — typically a few rows per business key (region, customer segment) feeding a specific dashboard or report. The two strongest signals: granularity (individual rows vs aggregated summary) and quality (raw vs cleaned). Format (CSV vs Parquet) and source (API vs SCADA) are NOT the deciding factors.
description.task: Classify each dataset into Bronze, Silver, or Gold.
description.validationHint: Each layer appears at least once. Think about what has been done to the data — nothing, cleaned, or aggregated.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four datasets from NordGrid's data lake; classify each by layer.

fields.label: Dataset A: A JSON file from the external weather API containing temperature readings for all NordGrid regions. The file is stored exactly as the API returned it, with no type conversions, no validation, and no deduplication.
options: Bronze — 'stored exactly as the API returned it' is the textbook signal of a raw landing zone; no transformations have been applied.
Silver — weather data is reference/lookup data, so it goes in Silver alongside other reference tables.
Gold — JSON from an external API is consumed directly by dashboards, so it is business-ready.
Neither — external API data lives outside the medallion architecture entirely.
fields.correctAnswer: Bronze — 'stored exactly as the API returned it' is the textbook signal of a raw landing zone; no transformations have been applied.
fields.rationale: Bronze is defined by the absence of transformations.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Silver requires cleaning and conforming; this dataset has neither.

fields.label: Dataset B: A Parquet file containing meter readings where the daily_kw column is a proper numeric type, rows with null meter_id have been removed, negative energy values have been filtered out, and each row includes the substation_name from the reference table.
options: Bronze — Parquet files are storage-format optimizations, but the data inside is still the raw meter readings.
Silver — types are correct, invalid rows are filtered, reference data is joined, and granularity is still per-meter-per-day; this is the textbook Silver profile.
Gold — data with a strict schema and proper types is business-ready by definition.
Bronze — joining with substation_name is a Silver-style transformation, but everything else is raw.
fields.correctAnswer: Silver — types are correct, invalid rows are filtered, reference data is joined, and granularity is still per-meter-per-day; this is the textbook Silver profile.
fields.rationale: Silver = cleaned + conformed + still at original granularity.Every Silver signal is present (typed, validated, joined with reference).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Type casting and filtering are NOT raw; the dataset has been transformed.
Option C: Strict schema does not make data Gold; aggregation does.

fields.label: Dataset C: A table with exactly four rows — one per region — showing the total daily energy consumption, the count of active meters, and the average daily_kw for the operations dashboard.
options: Bronze — operations dashboards consume data directly from the source, so this is a Bronze passthrough.
Silver — the columns total, count, and average are derived from clean meter data, which is a Silver-style derivation.
Gold — four aggregated rows feeding a specific business dashboard is the textbook Gold profile.
Mixed — the table is Silver because it is per-region but Gold because it has aggregations.
fields.correctAnswer: Gold — four aggregated rows feeding a specific business dashboard is the textbook Gold profile.
fields.rationale: Gold = aggregated + business-ready + named consumer.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Bronze is raw landings; aggregated tables cannot be Bronze.

fields.label: Dataset D: A raw CSV file of SCADA turbine sensor readings containing columns rpm, temp, and ts. Some rows have negative rpm values from sensor malfunctions. The file was copied from the SCADA system without modification.
options: Bronze — copied without modification, raw, with quality issues preserved (negative rpm); these are the textbook Bronze signals.
Silver — sensor data has a typed schema (rpm, temp, ts) so it qualifies as conformed.
Gold — SCADA data feeds turbine dashboards, so it is business-ready by purpose.
Quarantine — data with known quality issues should be in a separate quarantine layer, not Bronze.
fields.correctAnswer: Bronze — copied without modification, raw, with quality issues preserved (negative rpm); these are the textbook Bronze signals.
fields.rationale: Bronze PRESERVES quality issues; it does not fix them.'Copied without modification' is the literal definition of a Bronze landing.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: A typed schema is necessary but not sufficient for Silver; cleaning must have happened.

tasks.title: Trace a Spark Job Through Execution

description.context: Spark uses LAZY EVALUATION: transformations (filter, withColumn, join, select) only BUILD a plan — they do not run anything. The plan executes only when an ACTION is called (write, count, show, collect, etc.). This means spark.read.parquet() does NOT actually read the file; it just records 'I will need to read this'. The read is deferred until an action triggers the whole plan. Inside the plan, transformations are split into STAGES separated by SHUFFLES. Narrow transformations (filter, withColumn, select) do not move data between executors and stay in the same stage. Wide transformations (groupBy, join, distinct, repartition) require a shuffle and start a new stage.
description.task: Predict the execution behavior of the pipeline below.
description.validationHint: Remember that Spark uses lazy evaluation — transformations build a plan, and only actions trigger execution.

evidence.label: Pipeline code
evidence.content:
scada = spark.read.parquet('bronze/scada/2026-03-22/')
scada = scada.filter(col('turbine_id').isNotNull())
scada = scada.filter(col('rpm') >= 0)
scada = scada.withColumn('temp', col('temp').cast('double'))
turbine_ref = spark.read.csv('bronze/turbine_reference.csv', header=True)
scada = scada.join(turbine_ref, 'turbine_id', 'left')
scada.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('silver/scada/2026-03-22/')

fields.label: How many actions in this pipeline trigger execution?
fields.rationale: The only action is write.parquet(). The read, filter, withColumn, and join lines are transformations that build the plan but do not trigger execution.

fields.label: When does Spark actually start reading the Parquet file from disk?
options: When spark.read.parquet() runs — read is the one transformation that is NOT lazy because it must produce a DataFrame for the next line.
When the first filter() runs — filter cannot evaluate its predicate without actually reading the rows.
When join() runs — joins materialize both sides of the operation, so that is when both reads happen.
When write.parquet() runs — the action triggers the entire plan, so all reads, filters, and joins execute together at that moment.
fields.correctAnswer: When write.parquet() runs — the action triggers the entire plan, so all reads, filters, and joins execute together at that moment.
fields.rationale: Lazy evaluation means NO transformation runs until an action triggers the plan.
fields.distractorRationale:
read is lazy like every other transformation.
Option B: filter records a predicate; it does not pull data.

fields.label: Which operation creates a shuffle boundary between stages?
options: filter(col('turbine_id').isNotNull()) — filtering rearranges rows so unfiltered ones can be grouped together for the next step.
withColumn('temp', col('temp').cast('double')) — type casting requires Spark to collect all values to verify they cast cleanly, which is a shuffle.
join(turbine_ref, 'turbine_id', 'left') — rows with the same turbine_id from both DataFrames must be co-located on the same executor, which requires a shuffle.
write.parquet() — writing to disk requires collecting all data on the driver first, which counts as a shuffle.
fields.correctAnswer: join(turbine_ref, 'turbine_id', 'left') — rows with the same turbine_id from both DataFrames must be co-located on the same executor, which requires a shuffle.
fields.rationale: A shuffle is required when matching keys must end up on the same executor.join is the canonical wide transformation.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: filter operates row-by-row in place — the narrowest of narrow transformations.

fields.label: How many stages does this job produce?
fields.rationale: Stage 1: read Parquet, filter nulls, filter negative RPM, cast temp (all narrow transformations, no data movement).Shuffle boundary at the join.

tasks.title: Trace NordGrid's Meter Pipeline End to End

description.context: Every Spark job exists because of one root cause: a single machine cannot fit, read, or process the data fast enough. That triggers the move to a CLUSTER, where the DRIVER runs the Python code and orchestrates work, while EXECUTORS run the actual tasks on partitions. Data flows through three layers: Bronze (raw landing), Silver (cleaned per-record), Gold (aggregated business summary). This task walks through one full pipeline — from why distribution is needed at all, to where the data ends up — testing each concept once.
description.task: Trace the expanded pipeline through NordGrid's complete architecture, from single-machine bottleneck to medallion layers.
description.validationHint: This task spans concepts from across the entire module. Each question is independent — a correct answer on one does not depend on another.

fields.label: The expanded daily meter file is 2.2 GB. On the team's 16 GB development server, a Pandas script crashes with MemoryError when loading this file. Which wall is responsible?
options: Disk I/O — the SSD cannot read 2.2 GB in one allocation, so Python aborts with MemoryError to indicate the read failed.
Memory — the 2.2 GB CSV expands 3-5x into Python objects (roughly 10 GB working set), and other processes consume the rest of the 16 GB; the OS denies the allocation and Python crashes.
Compute — 750,000 rows is too many for a single CPU to parse line-by-line, so Pandas raises MemoryError to signal CPU exhaustion.
Network — the file transfer from the source system times out, and Pandas wraps the timeout as a MemoryError.
fields.correctAnswer: Memory — the 2.2 GB CSV expands 3-5x into Python objects (roughly 10 GB working set), and other processes consume the rest of the 16 GB; the OS denies the allocation and Python crashes.
fields.rationale: MemoryError ALWAYS indicates the OS denied a memory allocation.Disk and CPU walls cause slowness, not crashes.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Slow reads cause delays, never MemoryError.
Option C: CPU exhaustion produces slowness, not allocation failures.

fields.label: The team deploys the pipeline on a Spark cluster with 6 executors. When the PySpark script runs, which component builds the execution plan and assigns tasks to executors?
options: The executors — they elect a leader among themselves who coordinates work distribution.
The cluster manager (YARN/Kubernetes) — it owns the plan and tells executors what to run.
The driver — it runs the Python code, builds the DAG, requests executors from the cluster manager, and assigns tasks to them.
The Py4J bridge — it translates Python into JVM bytecode and runs as the orchestrator.
fields.correctAnswer: The driver — it runs the Python code, builds the DAG, requests executors from the cluster manager, and assigns tasks to them.
fields.rationale: The driver is the brain of the Spark application.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Executors do not self-coordinate; they receive tasks from the driver.

fields.label: The raw 2.2 GB meter CSV arrives from the source system and is stored without any cleaning, type casting, or validation. Which medallion architecture layer does this raw file belong to?
options: Bronze — raw data stored exactly as it arrived, with all quality issues preserved; this is the textbook Bronze landing.
Silver — once data is in the lake, it is by definition Silver because it has been 'received'.
Gold — the meter file feeds the pipeline that produces the dashboard, so it is upstream of Gold and inherits the label.
Staging — raw arrival files belong in a staging layer that sits before Bronze.
fields.correctAnswer: Bronze — raw data stored exactly as it arrived, with all quality issues preserved; this is the textbook Bronze landing.
fields.rationale: Bronze = raw, untouched, quality issues preserved.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: 'Received' is not a transformation; Silver requires actual cleaning.
Option C: Pipeline lineage does not change a layer's classification.

fields.label: After the pipeline filters invalid readings, casts daily_kw to a numeric type, and joins with the substation reference table, the result is stored as a Parquet file with a strict schema. Which layer does this output belong to?
options: Bronze — it derives from the raw file, and lineage determines the layer.
Silver — cleaned, typed, validated, joined with reference data, still per-meter granularity; this is the textbook Silver profile.
Gold — strict-schema Parquet with reference data joined IS the dashboard input, so it qualifies as Gold.
Both Silver and Gold — it serves as Silver for some pipelines and Gold for others.
fields.correctAnswer: Silver — cleaned, typed, validated, joined with reference data, still per-meter granularity; this is the textbook Silver profile.
fields.rationale: Silver = cleaned + conformed + per-record granularity.All Silver signals are present.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Lineage does not determine layer; transformation state does.

fields.label: The pipeline's final output is a summary table with one row per region (NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST) showing total daily energy and active meter count for the operations dashboard. Which layer is this?
options: Bronze — the regions and totals are derived from raw data, so they preserve raw lineage.
Silver — the columns are validated energy readings aggregated to a clean schema.
Gold — four aggregated rows feeding a named business consumer (operations dashboard) is the textbook Gold profile.
Reporting — aggregated dashboard tables belong in a separate Reporting layer outside the medallion.
fields.correctAnswer: Gold — four aggregated rows feeding a named business consumer (operations dashboard) is the textbook Gold profile.
fields.rationale: Gold = aggregated + named consumer.Three signals: aggregation (sum, count), few rows (4 vs 500K), specific consumer (operations dashboard).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Lineage does not preserve a layer label; transformation state does.
Option B: Aggregation across records moves data from Silver to Gold.
